COVID LOCKDOWN Property Market Reboot

By: Julian Sun | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How to restart the property market

Unique Selling Point:
What will it take to bring the housing market back from the brink?

Summary:
As lockdown restrictions ease in coming months, the property market that’s been frozen - not only because of the COVD-19 lockdown, but also because of the dismal economy - needs to be brought back to life. We investigate how everyone in the homebuying supply chain - from agents, to buyers to sellers and conveyance attorneys have been hamstrung by the closing of the deeds office - in some cases with unimaginable consequences.

Press Release:


Home Sales in Lockdown
Already in freefall before the COVID-19 lockdown, the property market has been all but frozen by the temporary closing of the Deeds Office. Carte Blanche investigates the unintended consequences that have followed as home sales have been hindered by restrictions on moving – and asks what it will take to re-start this sector of the economy.

Script:



INTRO VOICE OVER: Buying a home is a rite of passage and for many, one of the biggest commitments they’ll make in their lives. It offers the potential for financial stability and security.

The housing market was already in a slump due to the recession, now the lockdown caused by COVID-19 has thrown real estate into the biggest crisis it has ever faced.


OPENING LINK: The Deeds Office is where the transfer of houses from old to new owner happens. However when South Africa went into lockdown, Deeds Offices all over the country shut down freezing the property market.




V/O: Anastasia Haji Pavlou is a conveyance attorney. She relies on a properly functioning deeds office to be able to do her job.

· She explains what the deeds office does
· Mentions other cogs of the wheel that have been affected by lockdown: electrical compliance certificates & SARS


V/O: The 9 Deeds Offices around the country shut when South Africa went into lockdown, in effect seizing the engine that drives the property market.

This has had a devastating impact on real estate agents like Deena Pittum

· Deena talks about the impact of the deeds office has had on her business whilst South Africa was in level 5 lockdown

V/O: When the lockdown was lowered to level four, deeds offices were supposed to reopen this week but this still has not happened. Michelle Dickens from the TPN credit bureau explains why.

· Michelle explains why deeds offices haven’t reopened yet
· Also explains the implications of a level 4 lockdown


LINK: Buying a house is a dream for many but because of Covid-19 that dream has turned into a nightmare for many South Africans.

· Deena explains how some of her clients have been affected by the lockdown

V/O: We went to visit one of these empty houses.

V/O: They say that after death and divorce, moving house is one of life’s most stressful events.

That’s been doubly so for Tracy (not her real name). She was threatened by the person she sold her house to and has been so traumatized by the experience, she asked that her true identity be hidden for fear of reprisals.

V/O: After she sold, Tracy bought a new home, but has not been able to move in because the existing owners are still living there (due to lockdown restrictions)

But the new owner of her house insisted on occupation on the 1st of May, threatening to throw Tracy onto the street when he moved in. In desperation, she’s been forced to rent another property just to get out of the house.

· Tracy tells the story of her ordeal

V/O: But according to attorney Cilna Steyn it is illegal to forcibly evict someone during level 4 lockdown

· Cilna of the illegality of evictions and moving during level 4

V/O: The lockdown is having severe consequences on the economy, with many people unable to pay their rent. So what recourse do they have?

· Cilna on the rights of landlords and tenants










We bring back Michelle Dickens here to talk about the default rates that are occurring now.




V/O: But then on Thursday, a ray of hope for those able to move: The government relaxed level 4 regulations. People and their household effects may move around South Africa on a once-off basis between now and the 7th of June.

This applies to those who entered a new lease agreement, either before or during lockdown, or those that have bought new homes and the transfer of the property has already gone through.

In order to move, you will need to obtain a permit from your local police station, along with a copy of the signed lease agreement or transfer.

Unfortunately this doesn’t help Tracy, as the house she purchased still needs to be transferred into her name.

V/O: With interest rates slashed, it should be a good time to buy, but despite deeds offices reopening, real estate agents won’t be able to work until level 2 restrictions

This has everyone in the value chain worried. Property Agent Herschel Jawitz fears for the future of his business

· Herschel on the impact on his business
· Deena on not knowing when she’ll be able to work again
· Anastasia fearing for her company

Final comment from Vanessa
TEASER: As COVID-19 lockdown restrictions begin to ease in coming months – how will the all-but-frozen-property market, squeezed by lingering economic recession – begin to return to life?

PROMO: The property market has been frozen by the lockdown that threatens the very security that buying a home is supposed to give. We investigate the greatest crisis that Real Estate has ever faced.



Promo 2: Moving house is stressful enough but moving during a pandemic is a nightmare. Thousands of South Africans face an uncertain future, as movement restrictions continue and property transfers remain in limbo.


Promo 3: Imagine buying a home but because of lockdown, it can’t be transferred into your name and you’re not allowed to move in. That‘s the nightmare scenario playing out for thousands of South Africans upended by Covid-19.
